newsitem.title: CONGO: Zaire war foes head for talks at sea with Mandela.
newsitem.headline: Zaire war foes head for talks at sea with Mandela.

text.p: Zaire's ailing president, Mobutu Sese Seko, and civil war foe Laurent Kabila headed for talks at sea on Friday on a converted ice-breaker under the chairmanship of South Africa's Nelson Mandela.

Mandela, who has staked his reputation on brokering a peaceful end to the war at the face-to-face talks, met Mobutu at the port of Pointe Noire on Congo's coast to escort him to the talks, airports officials there said.
Kabila was in Angola's capital Luanda holding talks with President Eduardo dos Santos, government sources there said.
He was scheduled to join Mobutu and Mandela later on the South African naval vessel SAS Outeniqua in international waters off the Atlantic coast of Central Africa.
"I am convinced personally that both of them do want a settlement," Mandela told reporters before leaving South Africa for Pointe Noire to escort Mobutu on board.
"If I was not optimistic I wouldn't be going there. I am going because I feel the possibility of a movement forward is there."
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis living there, control about three quarters of Zaire and are marching on the capital Kinshasa.
Kabila, who says Mobutu must stand down after three decades in power, has refused to declare a truce for the talks.
Confusion over timing plagued the runup to the meeting, which diplomats see as a last chance to avert a potentially bloody battle for Zaire's capital of five million people.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.

Mobutu's camp says the talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a facer-save to allow the veteran strongman, who has cancer, to stand down with dignity.
Kabila, 56, insists Mobutu must go. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said on Wednesday.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who helped Mandela bring the two sides together, has said there are no conditions for the talks.

South Africa's ambassador to Zaire, Jan van Beventer, told reporters waiting in Pointe Noire to board the Outeniqua that all the major players were expected to show and the talks were expected to last just one day.

"We are going to try to get it done today but anything can happen," he said. "We are busy with a very, very serious situation. You know the rebels have taken most of Zaire... (The two sides) have got to sort their problem out for themselves."
Kabila and Mandela's deputy, Thabo Mbeki, were expected to travel by helicopter to join the ship in international waters off Soyo near the border between Angola and Zaire.
Mobutu, 66, had prostate cancer surgery in August. He seized power in 1965 and since then has dominated what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries.
Opponents denounce rampant corruption and administrative chaos and accuse Mobutu and his entourage of amassing fortunes while the bulk of the population floundered in poverty.
South Africa bought the Russian-built Outeniqua, dubbed "The Grey Diplomat", in 1993. It uses it as a naval supply vessel.
